Standardise a variable or scale it to a percentage

Source: R/std.R
std.Rd

Vector helpers for dplyr::mutate(), following Stata's egen:

  • std(): Standardise to mean 0 and standard deviation 1, like egen z = std(x). Unlike scale(), it returns a plain vector.

  • pc(): Express each value as a percentage of the total, like egen p = pc(x), or as a proportion with prop = TRUE.

Usage

std(x, mean = 0, sd = 1)

pc(x, prop = FALSE)

Arguments

x

A numeric or logical vector. Labelled numeric vectors are used through their codes.

mean, sd

For std(), finite numeric scalars giving the target mean (default 0) and signed scale multiplier (default 1), like Stata's egen std(x), mean() std() options. The result has standard deviation abs(sd); a negative sd reverses the ordering and zero makes all observed values equal to mean when the input spread is defined.

prop

If TRUE, pc() returns proportions (summing to 1) instead of percentages (summing to 100). Defaults to FALSE.

Value

A double vector with the length and order of x. Input classes, names, and labels are dropped; tagged and SPSS user-missing values are treated as missing. Missing inputs remain missing. std() returns all NA when the standard deviation is zero or undefined (fewer than two observed values), and pc() when the total is zero or infinite, as Stata gives missing values there.

Details

By default, std(x) computes (x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)) / sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) using the sample standard deviation. pc(x) computes 100 * x / sum(x, na.rm = TRUE), not percentile ranks. Use dplyr::percent_rank() for ranks on a 0-1 scale, or multiply them by 100 for a 0-100 scale. In grouped dplyr::mutate() (or with .by), the mean, standard deviation and total come from each group, like Stata's by g: egen.

See also

Other variable generation functions: as_dummy(), cut_quantile(), panel, row_egen, stata_recode()

Examples

std(c(1, 2, 3, NA))
#> [1] -1  0  1 NA

pc(c(2, 3, 5))
#> [1] 20 30 50

pc(c(2, 3, 5), prop = TRUE)
#> [1] 0.2 0.3 0.5

lifeexp |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    z = std(lexp),
    share = pc(popgrowth),
    .by = region
  )
#> # A tibble: 68 × 8
